title: Connected by a trail. United by its future.
summary: The Alliance brings people together to promote, preserve, and protect the Iditarod National Historic Trail.
body:
The Iditarod Historic Trail Alliance is a statewide nonprofit organization founded in 1999. Its work connects education, history, recreation, and stewardship.

Through partnerships with communities, landowners, agencies, and volunteers, the Alliance helps keep the trail’s heritage present and its future possible.

title: Seward & Resurrection Bay
summary: Begin where the mountains meet the sea.
body: At the southern end of the historic route, Seward offers an approachable connection to the trail. Start with the waterfront, discover local history, and explore the relationship between a coastal community and the journeys that began here.

title: Chugach country
summary: Find a new perspective in Southcentral Alaska.
body: The southern trail passes through a landscape of mountains, forests, and water. Explore official visitor resources for the Chugach region and historic trail connections, including Crow Pass. Choose an outing suited to your experience and check with the relevant land manager before setting out.

title: The winter trail
summary: Experience the season that shaped the trail.
body: Snow and frozen ground connect a landscape that changes dramatically through the year. Skiers, dog teams, snowmachines, and winter cyclists continue a long relationship with winter travel. Remote sections require substantial preparation and local knowledge; begin with the BLM visitor resources.

fields.credit: Winter cycling on the Iditarod Trail · Bob Wick / BLM

title: A living connection across Alaska
summary: The story of the trail begins with connection: between places, between people, and between generations.
body:
Long before a named gold-rush route appeared on maps, Alaska Native travel networks connected communities across this landscape. Those connections belong at the beginning of the trail's story, and remain part of its living present.

Later, the movement of mail, supplies, and people linked coastal ports and Interior settlements. The trail carries many histories, shaped by the communities along it and the seasons that make travel possible.

Preserving this heritage means listening as well as looking. The University of Alaska Fairbanks' Project Jukebox brings together recorded voices and personal perspectives. Follow those stories to learn from the people who know the trail.

fields.image_alt: Winter light on mountains and spruce along the Iditarod Trail

title: The winter way
summary: For generations, winter has opened a way across Alaska.
body:
A winter trail is a relationship with a changing landscape. Snow, frozen rivers, and seasonal knowledge shape where and how people travel.

Dog teams are part of that story. So are the people who maintain routes, share knowledge, and connect neighboring communities. Today the trail also welcomes different forms of recreation, from skiing to winter cycling.

The historic trail is a network, with different landowners, conditions, and access requirements. Learning about it is an invitation to understand the landscape before planning a journey through it.

fields.image_alt: A sled dog team resting on straw in the snow

title: The next generation of trail stories
summary: A place becomes more meaningful when we learn how to care for it.
body:
A trail can be an outdoor classroom. Observing a landscape, asking about a place name, and listening to a local story can open new ways of understanding where we live.

The Alliance's Iditarod Trail to Every Classroom program connects place-based learning with stewardship and community. Its existing resources offer starting points for educators and curious families.

Explore the Junior Trailblazer materials, discover a passport stamp location, or browse the education program. Start with a question, then follow it somewhere new.
